$comment: The real chutescoder binary, run end to end with RLM mode on. Every value here is read off reports/binary_ab/{summary.jsonl,C-chutescoder.jsonl} and the session rollout for thread 019fd4dc-b4d5-73c2-bc87-fd45e5379f82. Deliberately NO timing comparison between the arms: n = 1 per arm, and this page carries no performance claim in either direction.
endpoint: our own responses-proxy instance (production still has the multi-turn bug)
task: A fixture repo whose parser drops the last line when the input has no trailing newline. Two tests, one failing. Fix parser.py, do not touch the tests.
question: Does the shipped binary — not a driver we wrote — actually boot the kernel, execute Python and finish a real task with the flag on?
outcome: completed — both tests pass, tests unmodified

timeline.text: `chutescoder exec` starts with `-c rlm.enabled=true`, provider `chutes`, model `moonshotai/Kimi-K3-TEE`. The IPython sidecar boots.
`print(list_dir(".", depth=2))` — a real host call, routed back through Codex's own tool registry.
Reads both files in **one** cell and binds them to variables, then names the bug: `text.split("\n")[:-1]` unconditionally drops the final element.

Tries `apply_patch(...)` from inside Python. The host returns `HostError: unsupported call: apply_patch` — an explicit error, not a plausible-looking empty result — and the model switches to `write_file` in the next cell.
Runs the tests, hits the same pytest capture-teardown fault the earlier smoke run hit, and works around it with `--capture=no -p no:cacheprovider`.
Verifies with `git diff` from inside the kernel: only `parser.py` changed, both tests pass.

proves: The shipped binary works end to end with RLM mode on: the kernel boots, real Python executes, host calls route through Codex's existing tool registry, the error path surfaces failures explicitly, and the task is completed correctly. Arm B — the same binary with `rlm.enabled=false` — completed it too, so the flag does not break the product in either position.
does_not_prove: Nothing about which harness is better. This is n = 1 per arm on one small fixture task, and no timing or token comparison is drawn from it — see the retraction in section 04 for why n = 1 wall-clock differences are not reported here.
